**Banker's rounding** (also called round-half-to-even or round-half-even) is a tie-breaking rule. Values that aren't exactly halfway round to the nearest number as usual. When a value is exactly halfway, it rounds to the nearest **even** digit.

| Value | Round to integer |
|---|---|
| 2.4 | 2 |
| 2.6 | 3 |
| 2.5 | **2** (tie, goes to even) |
| 3.5 | **4** (tie, goes to even) |
| 0.125 → 2 decimals | 0.12 |
| 0.135 → 2 decimals | 0.14 |

This differs from the "round half up" taught in school, where every .5 goes up.

**Why accountants like it**

- **It avoids systematic bias.** Round-half-up always pushes ties upward. Over thousands of transactions, that adds a small but consistent upward drift. With round-half-even, ties go up about half the time and down about half the time, so the errors cancel out.
- **Totals stay closer to the true sum.** This matters when you round many line items, such as taxes, interest and currency conversions, and then aggregate them. Rounded totals reconcile better with unrounded ones.
- **It is a standard.** It is the default rounding mode in IEEE 754 floating point. It is also the default in many financial libraries, such as .NET's `Math.Round` and Python's `round()` and `decimal.ROUND_HALF_EVEN`. Some regulations and accounting standards call for it.

**Caveats**

- It only affects exact ties. With real-world data that has many decimal places, ties are rare. The effect shows up mainly with data that has fixed precision, such as prices and tax rates.
- Binary floating point can hide ties. For example, 2.675 isn't exactly representable, so it may not round the way you expect. For money, use a decimal type or integer cents.
- Reproducibility matters. If one system rounds half-up and another rounds half-even, their totals can differ by a cent. Pick one rule and apply it consistently.

An EngramDB memory surfaced for this project says tax uses `ROUND_HALF_EVEN`, so it's the same idea.
